# Enuresis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Urology > Urine retention and incontinence > Enuresis*

[Original Article Link](/library/HP0KTT)

---

## Summary

<u>Enuresis</u> or <u>bed-wetting</u> is the repeated voiding of urine during <u>sleep</u> in an individual with a developmental age ≥ 5 years. In <u>monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis</u> (<u>MNE</u>), wetting occurs only at night during <u>sleep</u>, while <u>nonmonosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis</u> (<u>NMNE</u>) manifests with daytime urinary symptoms (e.g., daytime incontinence, <u>urinary urgency</u>, difficulty voiding) in addition to nighttime wetting. <u>Enuresis</u> can be primary (nocturnal dryness has never been achieved) or secondary (symptom onset occurs after > 6 months of nocturnal dryness). <u>Primary MNE</u> is typically caused by a mismatch between <u>arousal from sleep</u> and nocturnal <u>urine production</u> and/or storage. <u>Secondary MNE</u> and <u>NMNE</u> are usually caused by psychological <u>stress</u> or medical conditions (e.g., <u>constipation</u>, <u>urinary tract infection</u>). <u>Risk factors</u> for <u>enuresis</u> include psychosocial factors, male sex, and positive <u>family history</u>. The diagnosis is clinical, based on the <u>DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for enuresis</u>. Initial management involves addressing the underlying cause, behavioral modification, use of an <u>enuresis alarm</u>, and/or <u>desmopressin</u>. Children with refractory symptoms or persistent daytime urinary symptoms should be evaluated and managed by a specialist (e.g., pediatric urology). <u>Enuresis</u> has a good prognosis with a high rate of spontaneous resolution.

---

## Definitions

* <u>Enuresis</u> (<u>bed-wetting</u>): repeated voiding of urine during <u>sleep</u> in an individual with a developmental age ≥ 5 years [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)[[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)

* Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis (<u>MNE</u>): <u>enuresis</u> without daytime <u>lower urinary tract symptoms</u> (<u>LUTS</u>) 

* <u>Primary MNE</u>: <u>enuresis</u> in which nocturnal dryness was never achieved

* <u>Secondary MNE</u>: <u>enuresis</u> in which symptom onset is after ≥ 6 months of nocturnal dryness

* <u>Nonmonosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis</u> (<u>NMNE</u>): <u>enuresis</u> and daytime <u>LUTS</u> (e.g., <u>urinary incontinence</u>, <u>urinary urgency</u>, change in voiding frequency, difficulty voiding)

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Enuresis</u> affects 5–10% of 7-year-olds [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)

* <u>Prevalence</u> decreases with age.  [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)

* <u>MNE</u> 

* Most common type

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)

* <u>NMNE</u>

* Accounts for 15–30% of cases [[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

There is significant overlap in the etiology of <u>MNE</u> and <u>NMNE</u>. For example, <u>constipation</u>, <u>detrusor</u> overactivity, and psychological conditions can cause <u>MNE</u> (primary or secondary) and <u>NMNE</u>. The most common causes for each type of <u>enuresis</u> are listed below. [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)




### Primary MNE [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)




<u>Primary MNE</u> is caused by a mismatch between <u>arousal from sleep</u> and nocturnal <u>urine production</u> and/or storage. <u>Risk factors</u> include positive <u>family history</u> and male sex. [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




* Delayed physiological maturation of the <u>brain</u>-<u>bladder</u> axis [[4]](/library/n-d7Bs0)

* Difficulty arousing from <u>sleep</u> in response to nocturnal <u>bladder</u> cues due to, e.g.:

* High <u>sleep arousal</u> threshold (deep sleeper) [[4]](/library/n-d7Bs0)[[5]](/library/tH1XHR0)

* <u>Obstructive sleep apnea</u> (commonly due to adenotonsillar <u>hypertrophy</u>)

* <u>Sleep arousal</u> disorder

* <u>Nocturnal polyuria</u> due to, e.g.:

* Excess fluid consumption before bedtime

* <u>Osmotic diuresis</u> (e.g., due to consumption of salty or sugary foods at night)

* Insufficient nocturnal <u>vasopressin</u> release

* Low <u>bladder</u> storage capacity





### Secondary MNE [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)[[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)[[5]](/library/tH1XHR0)




Causes of <u>secondary MNE</u> include:




* Psychological <u>stress</u> (e.g., recent move, <u>sexual abuse</u>, family conflicts)

* Underlying pathological conditions, e.g.:

* <u>Diabetes insipidus in children</u>

* <u>Diabetes mellitus in children</u>

* <u>Urinary tract infection in children</u>

* <u>Acute kidney failure</u>





### NMNE [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)




In addition to conditions that cause <u>secondary MNE</u>, <u>NMNE</u> can be caused by anatomical, neurological, and psychosocial disorders, e.g.:




* <u>Urinary tract</u> disorders

* <u>CAKUT</u>

* <u>Urinary tract obstruction</u>

* <u>Neurogenic bladder</u>

* <u>Overactive bladder</u>

* <u>Chronic kidney disease</u>

* <u>Constipation in children</u>

* <u>Neurodevelopmental disorders</u>;  (e.g., <u>attention deficit hyperactivity disorder</u>, <u>autism spectrum disorder</u>, <u>developmental delay</u>) [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)

* Psychiatric conditions (e.g., <u>conduct disorder</u>, <u>separation anxiety disorder</u>) [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)[[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)




* <u>Enuresis</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> based on <u>DSM-5</u> criteria.

* Obtain a comprehensive clinical history (including a 7-day <u>voiding diary</u> if appropriate) and perform a <u>physical examination</u> to:  [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)

* Distinguish between <u>MNE</u> and <u>NMNE</u>

* Assess symptom severity

* Evaluate for an underlying cause

* Consider diagnostic studies for an underlying cause in selected patients.





### DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for enuresis [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




All of the following criteria should be met to confirm the diagnosis.




* Voiding of urine into bed and/or clothing is repeated, involuntary or intentional, and occurs in an individual with a developmental age ≥ 5 years.  [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)

* Symptoms occur ≥ 2 times per week for ≥ 3 months or cause significant <u>distress</u> and/or adverse consequences (e.g., social ostracism, poor academic or occupational outcomes).

* Symptoms are not caused by medication or a medical condition.





### Evaluate for an underlying cause [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)




* Indications for diagnostic testing for an underlying cause include: [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)

* Daytime symptoms (i.e., <u>NMNE</u>)

* <u>Secondary MNE</u>

* Daytime <u>LUTS</u> and/or difficulty voiding

* <u>Excessive daytime sleepiness</u> or snoring

* <u>Growth faltering</u>

* <u>Constipation</u>, <u>fecal impaction</u>

* Lower extremity neurological abnormalities

* Sacral anomalies (e.g., sacral tuft or dimple)

* Obtain appropriate diagnostic studies based on clinical presentation, e.g.:

* <u>Urinalysis</u> to assess for <u>UTI</u>

* ENT evaluation for adenotonsillar <u>hypertrophy</u>

* <u>Diagnostics for obstructive sleep apnea</u>

* <u>Diagnostics for chronic kidney disease</u>

* <u>Diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus</u>

* <u>Diagnosis of constipation in children</u>





> [!TIP]
> Patients with <u>primary MNE</u> do not routinely require diagnostic evaluation for an underlying cause. [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)

---

## Management

### Approach [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)




* Address the psychological stressors and/or underlying conditions contributing to <u>enuresis</u>; see, e.g:  [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)

* <u>Management of constipation in children</u>

* <u>Management of UTI in children</u>

* <u>Management of obstructive sleep apnea</u>

* Refer patients with <u>NMNE</u> to pediatric urology for management of daytime symptoms and/or <u>LUTS</u>.  [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)

* Management of nocturnal symptoms

* Discuss behavioral modification strategies to reduce <u>enuresis</u>.

* Patients ≥ 6 years and/or those with <u>distress</u> or impaired social functioning due to <u>enuresis</u>:  [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0); ; 

* Initiate treatment with <u>enuresis alarm</u> or <u>desmopressin</u>; use <u>shared decision-making</u>.

* Consider switching or combining therapies based on symptom improvement.

* Refractory symptoms: Refer to pediatric urology for further evaluation and management.





> [!TIP]
> Treatment of <u>enuresis</u> is not routinely indicated for children < 5 years of age. [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




> [!TIP]
> An <u>enuresis alarm</u> and <u>desmopressin</u> are both effective first-line management strategies for <u>enuresis</u>. Use <u>shared decision-making</u> to select the appropriate treatment strategy.




### Behavioral modification [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)[[6]](/library/X-d9Ds0)




* Behavioral modification strategies to reduce <u>enuresis</u> include:  

* Fluid intake regulation (e.g., 30–50 mL/kg per day, minimizing fluid intake 1–2 hours before <u>sleep</u>) [[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)

* Timed <u>bladder</u> emptying during the day (e.g., every 3 hours) [[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)

* <u>Positive reinforcement</u> of proper voiding techniques

* Discourage use of unproven or punitive measures (e.g., waking the child at night to urinate).





### Enuresis alarm [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)




A moisture sensor in the child's underwear or sleeping pad triggers an alarm and/or vibration, alerting the child and/or caregiver when involuntary <u>urination</u> occurs.




* Indicated in children ≥ 6 years of age with frequent <u>enuresis</u>  [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)

* Consistent use without interruption is required.

* Follow-up within 6 weeks.

* Symptom improvement 

* Discontinue after 14 consecutive dry nights.

* Treatment may be resumed if symptoms recur.

* No improvement: Consider switching to or combining with other treatment strategies.





### <u>Desmopressin</u> [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)[[7]](/library/K-dUys0)




* Indicated in children ≥ 6 years:

* With <u>nocturnal polyuria</u>

* When rapid short-term improvement is desired (e.g., school trips)

* <u>Desmopressin</u> dosage considerations: DOSAGE 

* Consider if daily or periodic dosing (e.g., summer camp, sleepovers) is required.

* <u>Desmopressin</u> carries a rare but serious risk for <u>hyponatremia</u> and/or water intoxication. [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[7]](/library/K-dUys0)

* Withhold <u>desmopressin</u> after periods of increased water ingestion.

* Limit fluid intake to ≤ 200 mL within an hour of bedtime and throughout the night. [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)

* Children on continuous treatment: Follow-up every 2 weeks after initiating treatment.

* Improved symptoms

* Consider tapering <u>desmopressin</u> after 3 months of consistent improvement. [[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)

* Periodic <u>drug holidays</u> help determine when the medication can be stopped.

* No improvement: Consider switching to or combining with other treatment strategies.





### Refractory symptoms [[2]](/library/GxdBBH0)[[3]](/library/sxdtBH0)




Refer children with insufficient response to first-line therapies to pediatric urology for consideration of:




* Additional diagnostic evaluation (e.g., <u>urodynamic studies</u>)

* Alternative pharmacological treatment

* <u>Anticholinergics</u> (e.g., oxybutinin): considered in patients with <u>overactive bladder</u> as a likely cause

* <u>Imipramine</u>: associated with significant adverse effects (e.g., cardiotoxicity, <u>CNS</u> effects)

* Advanced therapies (e.g., peripheral nerve stimulation, intradetrusor <u>botulinum toxin</u> injection)
